subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Counting up to ten thousands with tokens and a chart

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences (a)–(i); discuss the patterns in class.

time_bands.activity: Distribute token cut-outs (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, and ten-thousands). Display a blank place-value chart on the board. Invite volunteers to place tokens representing 9,999 and ask what happens when one more is added — guide the class to merge ten 1,000-tokens into a single 10,000-token and name the new column TTh (ten-thousands). Have students read several 5-digit numbers placed on the chart aloud, discussing how the column position changes the value of each digit.

Write a range of 5-digit numbers on the board (e.g. 13,045; 50,302; 99,999). Students copy each number into their own place-value chart, filling one digit per column. Pairs read the numbers aloud using the Indian system number names, writing the name below each numeral. Choose a few for whole-class checking, explicitly correcting any confusion between the hundreds and thousands columns.

Introduce Let Us Do Q1, p.5 ("fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each sequence...."). Students work individually on parts (a)–(i), identifying the step size before filling each blank. Close with a quick class discussion: which sequences jump by equal steps, and which do not — reinforcing that reading the number correctly is the first move.

periods.teacher_notes: Students meeting the ten-thousands column for the first time often read 13,045 as 'one hundred and thirty thousand forty-five' — the token-merging demonstration directly counters this by making the column boundary visible. A common error in the sequence task is finding the wrong step size for sequences that alternate steps (e.g. +1,001); ask students to verify by computing the difference between the first two terms before continuing.
materials: Token cut-outs (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands) — one set per pair

periods.activity_title: Number-line ordering and the digit-position trap

tasks_in_class.description: Arrange the eight numbers (40,347; 34,407; 40,473; 34,740; 73,404; 74,430; 47,340; 18,926) in increasing order using the number line if required.
A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not? Use the number line and place value chart to fill in the blanks.
Digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478 to make a number larger than 5,500; in 10,593 to make numbers in given ranges; in 48,247 to make numbers as small/big as possible.

homework.description: Fill in the blanks appropriately: given a number write its number name, or given a name write the number; use commas as required.

time_bands.activity: Draw a 0–80,000 number line on the board, marking only the ten-thousands. Ask the class to suggest where 9,990 and 49,014 should sit. After students place the points, pose Let Us Do Q4, p.7 ("a student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4....") as an open question for pair discussion — the number line placement should immediately challenge the claim.

Introduce Let Us Do Q3, p.6 ("arrange the eight numbers in increasing order...."). Students first sort the eight numbers by their number of digits, then compare within each group column by column on a place-value chart. They mark all eight on the number line sketch and write the increasing order, noting that the number line confirms their column-by-column comparison.

Move to Let Us Do Q5, p.7 ("digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478...."). Students work in pairs, swapping pairs of digits systematically and checking each result against the target range using the place-value chart. Invite pairs to share which digit swap gave the largest or smallest result and why — drawing out the principle that the leftmost digit exerts the greatest influence on magnitude.

periods.teacher_notes: The chapter specifically flags the error of comparing by leading digit value alone (9,990 vs 49,014), making Q4 the conceptual centrepiece of this unit; encourage students to articulate why the number of digits matters before they compare individual digits. For the digit-swap task, students often swap the same digit with itself — prompt them to verify that their two chosen positions are different before checking the result.
materials: 0–80,000 number line (drawn on board or printed strip)

periods.activity_title: The hungry rabbit — rounding as a spatial act

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the rabbit fill-in (nearest hundred and nearest thousand of 2,346); fill in the table giving nearest tens, hundreds, and thousands for 3,176; 4,017; 5,789; 8,203.
Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used from 7,126; 7,835; 7,030; 6,999.

homework.description: Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten, (b) nearest hundred, (c) nearest thousand.

time_bands.activity: Draw a number line segment showing 2,300 and 2,400 with 2,346 marked between them. Use the hungry-rabbit story from the textbook: the rabbit is at 2,346 and its food is at the nearest hundred-mark — ask students to count jumps left and right to decide which benchmark is closer. Repeat for the nearest thousand (2,000 vs 3,000), making the spatial counting action the definition of rounding before any rule is named.

Work through Let Us Do (rounding table), p.8 ("complete the rabbit fill-in....") together for the first row, then let students complete the remaining three rows (3,176; 4,017; 5,789; 8,203) independently. Circulate and address cases where a number lies exactly in the middle of two benchmarks — introduce the convention that the midpoint rounds up.

Pose Let Us Think Q1, p.8 ("Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result....") to the class. Students test each of the four numbers individually on the number line, recording both roundings before circling the qualifying ones. Discuss what numerical property makes rounding to hundred and thousand give the same result — drawing out that only numbers where the hundreds digit is 0 can satisfy both.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 'nearest hundred' with 'the hundreds digit' — the spatial jump-count on the number line separates the procedure from the digit vocabulary. A frequent error in the rounding table is rounding 4,017 to the nearest ten as 4,020 rather than 4,020 (this is correct) but rounding 5,789 to the nearest hundred as 5,700 instead of 5,800 — have students recount jumps in both directions before committing.
materials: Number line segments (drawn on board for each rounding context)
Rounding table worksheet or textbook p.8

periods.activity_title: Rounding edge cases and travel-distance calculations

tasks_in_class.description: Think and write numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten and nearest hundred, (b) nearest hundred and nearest thousand, (c) nearest ten, hundred and thousand.
A cyclist covers 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours at the same speed?
A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them using modes (a) Bicycle(2) through (h) Aeroplane(180)?

homework.book_ref: Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11
homework.description: Find something in the textbook/classroom whose count is a 4-digit or 5-digit number; list quantities of 4- or 5-digit count in context of a tree and your village/town/city.

time_bands.activity: Open with Let Us Think Q3, p.9 ("think and write numbers that have the same nearest ten and nearest hundred...."). Students work in pairs, choosing numbers and testing each rounding on a number line sketch, gradually narrowing toward numbers that satisfy all three conditions simultaneously. Pairs share examples and the class builds a list on the board, discussing what structural feature (hundreds and tens digits both close to zero) satisfies condition (c).

Introduce the travel-speed table from page 10 briefly, reading selected speeds aloud. Students then solve Let Us Do Q1, p.10 ("a cyclist covers 15 km in one hour....") individually — a straightforward multiplication — and check by repeated addition. Follow with a quick show-of-hands: which travel modes have the class seen in real life?

Work through Let Us Do Q2, p.10 ("a school has 461 girls and 439 boys....") in small groups. Groups first add the totals (900), then divide by each vehicle capacity in turn. They record the number of vehicles needed and note when the division is inexact, discussing whether to round up or down in this real-world context. Select two or three vehicle modes for whole-class verification on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students transitioning from the rounding tasks to the division problems may try to round 900 before dividing — remind them that here the goal is an exact vehicle count, not an estimate. A common error in Q2 is rounding down when the division has a remainder, leaving some students without transport; ask 'can any child be left behind?' to anchor the rounding-up decision.

periods.activity_title: River crossing, pebble strategy, and the nine-pattern

tasks_in_class.description: River crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass across a river one at a time so neither the sheep eats grass nor the lion eats sheep; find minimum trips.
Pile of pebbles game (2 piles of 7 each; pick any number from one pile; last pebble wins): try the game with friends and find a winning strategy by starting with smaller piles.

Digit-swap subtraction puzzle: observe differences in each step; try other digit pairs; identify digits giving 1-digit number in first step; extend Mira's table for differences 2,3,5,7; find relationship between digit difference and number difference.

time_bands.activity: Present Pastime Mathematics Q1, p.11 ("river crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass...."). Students work in pairs, acting out the puzzle with labelled paper slips (lion, sheep, grass, boat). Encourage systematic listing of each crossing, tracking what is left on each bank at every step. After pairs find a solution, ask: is there more than one way — and what is the fewest number of trips needed?

Introduce Pastime Mathematics Q2, p.12 ("pile of pebbles game...."). Pairs use actual pebbles, counters, or torn paper pieces to play several rounds with piles of 7. Then reduce to smaller starting piles (1, 2, 3) and record which player wins with best play. Students discuss any emerging pattern in their findings, working toward a winning strategy they can state in words.

Guide the class through Pastime Mathematics Q3, p.12-13 ("digit-swap subtraction puzzle...."). Work through the first example as a class, recording the result in Mira's table. Small groups then try other digit pairs and fill in rows for differences 2, 3, 5, 7. Close by asking groups to state the relationship they found between the digit difference and the resulting number difference — inviting a generalisation rather than requiring a proof.

periods.teacher_notes: The river-crossing puzzle has a unique two-stage solution (sheep goes first, sheep returns on one leg); students who list moves systematically find it faster than those who guess — praise the listing strategy openly. For the digit-swap pattern, students sometimes confuse the digit difference (the gap between the two digits) with the number difference (the subtraction result) — keeping two labelled columns in the table prevents this conflation.
materials: Labelled paper slips for river-crossing (lion, sheep, grass)
Mira's table template (drawn in notebook or printed)

section_titles: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition

tasks_in_class.description: Write numbers 8,062; 9,980; 10,304; 23,004; 70,405 in expanded form.
Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions: e.g. 68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones; 607 = 4 Hundreds + __ Ones; 5,621 = 4 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 2 Tens + __ Ones; and similar (b)–(g).
Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934 and ₹65,342; how many thousands in each (b)–(h).

time_bands.activity: Write 70,405 on the board and ask students to read it aloud. Then ask: 'Can anyone write this as a sum of its place-value parts?' Build the expanded form column by column, emphasising that zero places must be omitted from the sum (70,000 + 400 + 5). Students then complete Let Us Do Q7, p.14 ("write numbers 8,062; 9,980; 10,304; 23,004; 70,405 in expanded form....") individually, paying attention to zeros.

Pose the first non-standard decomposition from Let Us Do Q8, p.14-15 ("68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones....") to the class. Demonstrate using a place-value chart: borrowing one ten from the tens column adds ten ones, keeping the total fixed. Students work through parts (b)–(g) in pairs, using the chart as a prop and explaining each step to their partner before writing the answer.

Introduce Let Us Do Q9, p.15 ("how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934...."). Frame it as a currency-desk task: how many notes of each denomination can you hand over? Students recognise this as a division of the amount by the note value, drawing the link to the non-standard decompositions above. Work through ₹7,934 in ₹10 notes together, then let students complete ₹65,342 and the thousands-counting sub-items.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent error in expanded form is writing the zero-place terms (e.g. '+ 0 Hundreds') — establish the convention that zero terms are dropped and ask students to check each other's work for this. In the non-standard decomposition tasks, students sometimes add extra value when they regroup; emphasise that regrouping trades one larger unit for ten smaller units, leaving the total unchanged.
materials: Play currency notes (₹10, ₹100, ₹500) or labelled cards

section_titles: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
periods.activity_title: Ordering large numbers and finding numbers between

tasks_in_class.description: Ravi's car: 56,987 km; Sheetal's car: 67,543 km. Whose car has been driven more?
Arrange town populations (65,232; 53,231; 56,380; 51,336; 45,858; 66,540) in descending (decreasing) order.
Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0.

homework.description: Write 5 numbers that are more than 38,125 but less than 38,600.

time_bands.activity: Present Let Us Do Q3, p.13 ("Ravi's car: 56,987 km; Sheetal's car: 67,543 km...."). Students compare column by column on a place-value chart, stating which digit position settles the comparison. Discuss: can we always stop at the first differing column from the left, and why?

Students complete Let Us Do Q4, p.13 ("arrange ₹90,000; ₹89,999; ₹94,983; ₹49,900; ₹93,743; ₹39,999 in ascending order....") and Let Us Do Q5, p.14 ("arrange town populations in descending order....") individually, using place-value charts as needed. Pairs then swap books and verify each other's ordering, correcting any sequence errors.

Pose Let Us Do Q6, p.14 ("find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0...."). Students first identify what form such a number must take (___,000), then list which thousands-multiples fall in the range. Discuss as a class: are there exactly the numbers students found, or could there be more — and what determines the count?

periods.teacher_notes: The comparison work in this unit consolidates the place-value comparison method introduced when studying comparing and ordering; students who struggled there benefit from the explicit column-by-column chart work before moving to listing. The Q6 constraint puzzle (ones, tens, hundreds all zero) is cognitively demanding — scaffold by first asking 'what does the number look like if those three digits are zero?' to expose the ___,000 structure.

periods.activity_title: Counting around the stable — shared corners and arrangement puzzles

tasks_in_class.description: Count horses in the given arrangement and find the caretaker's mistake; arrange 18 horses with 5 on each side; explore how many more can be stolen before the king notices.

time_bands.activity: Read the King's Horses story from p.15 aloud or paraphrase it. Draw the square stable arrangement on the board with 19 horses marked. Ask students to count the horses on each side independently, then total all four sides — and compare their total (20 if they count each corner twice) with the actual number of tokens. Guide the discussion to see that corner horses are shared by two sides, so counting per-side overcounts.

Challenge the class from King's Horses, p.15-16 ("arrange 18 horses with 5 on each side...."). Students use labelled counters on a drawn square-stable grid, experimenting with different corner and side distributions. Encourage recording each arrangement as (corner count, side count) and checking: 4 × corner + 4 × (side − 2 × corner) = total? Let students find multiple valid arrangements.

Extend to the exploration question: how many horses can be stolen one at a time while keeping exactly 5 on each side? Students test arrangements for 17, 16, and smaller totals, recording whether 5-per-side is still achievable. The class shares findings, noting the minimum total that still allows a 5-per-side arrangement — drawing out the combinatorial reasoning without requiring algebraic notation.

periods.teacher_notes: Students habitually add 5+5+5+5 and claim there are 20 horses — the deliberate over-count is the conceptual pivot of the puzzle; do not correct it prematurely, let the physical counter-placement reveal the double-counting. When students search for the minimum, they may not be systematic; suggest recording (corner, side) pairs in a small table to prevent revisiting arrangements already tried.
materials: Square stable grid drawn on paper (one per group)

section_titles: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
periods.activity_title: A journey through numbers — connecting place value, rounding, and reasoning

time_bands.activity: Present a 'Journey board' on the blackboard: six city distances written as 5-digit numbers (e.g. 23,405 km; 7,890 km; 45,010 km; 9,999 km; 60,300 km; 38,750 km). Students read each number aloud, write it in words, and place it in expanded form beside it. A quick round-robin checks that every student can move fluently between numeral, number name, and expanded form — drawing on reading and writing large numbers and the expanded form work.

Ask students to arrange the six journey distances in increasing order using a place-value chart, then round each to the nearest thousand and re-order the rounded values — checking whether the order is preserved. Discuss any case where rounding changed the relative position of two numbers, connecting rounding to the comparing-and-ordering understanding and the nearest-tens-hundreds-thousands procedures.

Pose a short synthesis problem: 'A train travels 15,000 km total. It stops at four cities. Using the distances from the Journey board, pick any two stops whose rounded-to-thousands distances add to exactly 15,000 km. Can you find more than one pair?' Students work individually, applying large-number arithmetic and estimation in a realistic travel context — drawing on finding large numbers around us.

Close with a non-standard decomposition challenge tied to the King's Horses spatial idea: write 15,000 in as many ways as possible using only thousands and hundreds (e.g. 15 Thousands + 0 Hundreds; 14 Thousands + 10 Hundreds; …). Students list arrangements systematically, noting the pattern — each trade of one thousand for ten hundreds is a step in a sequence, mirroring the combinatorial thinking from the stable puzzle. Share findings and discuss what pattern governs all valid decompositions.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together reading and writing large numbers, comparing and ordering, rounding, travel-context arithmetic, expanded form, non-standard decomposition, and combinatorial spatial reasoning — all chapter strands meet in the Journey board and the final decomposition challenge. A productive synthesis error to watch for: students rounding before comparing instead of comparing exact values first — address by asking 'which answer does the question actually need, the rounded value or the exact value?'
materials: Journey board (six distances written on blackboard)

items.prompt: Look at your mathematics textbook. Count the number of words on any one full page and write the count. Is it a 3-digit, 4-digit, or 5-digit number? Write the number name for your count.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Answers will vary. Accept any reasonable 3- or 4-digit count. The student should correctly identify the number of digits and write the matching Indian-system number name (e.g. 'two thousand three hundred forty-five' for 2,345).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count objects, record the numeral, and write the number name using the Indian place-value system.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count only one column of words first; stretch: ask them to estimate the total for the whole page and write it in expanded form.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11
exercise.description: Find something in the textbook/classroom whose count is a 4-digit or 5-digit number; list quantities of 4- or 5-digit count in context of a tree and your village/town/city.

items.prompt: Look at the number sequence below and write the next three numbers. Explain the rule you used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 14,003; 15,004; 16,005. The rule is add 1,001 each time.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the difference between consecutive terms, confirm it is constant, and add it repeatedly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to subtract 11,000 from 12,001 to find the step before continuing; stretch: ask them to write the tenth term in the sequence without listing all terms in between.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences (a)–(i); discuss the patterns in class.

items.prompt: Priya says 8,765 is greater than 28,104 because the digit 8 is greater than the digit 2. Is Priya correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because 28,104 has five digits and 8,765 has only four digits, so 28,104 is greater.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because we should always compare the ones digits first.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because the thousands digit of 8,765 is larger.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 28,104 is greater because it has five digits while 8,765 has only four digits.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the number of digits first; a number with more digits is always greater.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student compares leading digits without considering how many digits each number has — the same misconception the chapter directly addresses.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises a thousands digit but does not see that a five-digit number's leading digit sits in the ten-thousands place, not the thousands place.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student reverses the correct comparison direction, starting from ones instead of the leftmost digit.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write both numbers in a place-value chart and count the columns each fills; stretch: ask them to write a four-digit number that is greater than 20,000 — and explain why that is impossible.

exercise.description: A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not? Use the number line and place value chart to fill in the blanks.

items.prompt: The number 32,506 has its digits 3 and 5 swapped to make a new number. Write the new number. Is it larger or smaller than 32,506? Use a place-value chart to explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Swapping the digits 3 (ten-thousands) and 5 (hundreds) gives 52,306. This is larger than 32,506 because the ten-thousands digit changed from 3 to 5, and the ten-thousands place has the greatest value.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place both numbers in a place-value chart and compare from the leftmost column; the ten-thousands digit settles the comparison.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a blank place-value chart and ask the student to fill in both numbers before comparing; stretch: ask them to find a second digit-swap in 32,506 that makes the number as small as possible.

exercise.description: Digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478 to make a number larger than 5,500; in 10,593 to make numbers in given ranges; in 48,247 to make numbers as small/big as possible.

items.prompt: Meena rounded a number to the nearest hundred and got 7,000. Rajan rounded the same number to the nearest thousand and also got 7,000. Which number could they both have used?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — 7,038. Nearest hundred: 7,038 rounds to 7,000. Nearest thousand: 7,038 rounds to 7,000. Both match.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each candidate to the nearest hundred and then to the nearest thousand; select the number where both results equal 7,000.

what_each_option_reveals.D: 7,489 rounds to 7,500 (nearest hundred), not 7,000 — the student may have rounded only to the nearest thousand (7,000) and stopped.
what_each_option_reveals.B: 6,842 rounds to 6,800 (nearest hundred) and 7,000 (nearest thousand) — the student found one rounding correct but did not check both.
what_each_option_reveals.A: 6,550 rounds to 6,600 (nearest hundred) and 7,000 (nearest thousand) — same error pattern as B.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to mark each option on a number line segment between 6,500 and 7,500 before rounding; stretch: ask them to write all two-digit stems (tens and ones) that would make a 7,0__  number round to 7,000 for both benchmarks.

exercise.description: Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used from 7,126; 7,835; 7,030; 6,999.

items.prompt: Write one number whose nearest ten and nearest hundred are the same. Explain on a number line why this is true.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any number between 950 and 1,049 whose nearest ten and nearest hundred both equal 1,000 works — for example, 998 (nearest ten: 1,000; nearest hundred: 1,000). The student should mark 998 between 990 and 1,000 on a number line, showing it is closer to 1,000 for tens, and between 900 and 1,000 for hundreds, again closer to 1,000.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find a number whose nearest-ten benchmark and nearest-hundred benchmark coincide, and confirm by counting jumps on a number line in both directions.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student the number 998 and ask only for the number-line explanation; stretch: ask them to find a number between 1,000 and 2,000 where nearest ten, nearest hundred, and nearest thousand are all the same.

exercise.description: Think and write numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten and nearest hundred, (b) nearest hundred and nearest thousand, (c) nearest ten, hundred and thousand.

items.prompt: You must cross a river in a small boat that holds only you and one item. You have a dog, a chicken, and a bag of grain. The dog will eat the chicken if left alone together, and the chicken will eat the grain if left alone together. Describe your crossing plan step by step and state the minimum number of one-way trips needed.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Take the chicken across (trip 1). Return alone (trip 2). Take the dog across (trip 3). Bring the chicken back (trip 4). Take the grain across (trip 5). Return alone (trip 6). Take the chicken across (trip 7). Total: 7 one-way trips. (An equivalent solution swapping dog and grain in trips 3 and 5 is also valid.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List each trip systematically, checking after every crossing that no unsafe pair is left together on either bank.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student labelled paper slips for dog, chicken, and grain to act out each crossing physically; stretch: ask whether the puzzle can be solved in fewer than 7 trips, and justify the answer.

exercise.description: River crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass across a river one at a time so neither the sheep eats grass nor the lion eats sheep; find minimum trips.

items.prompt: Choose any two-digit number whose digits are different (for example, 63). Reverse its digits (36). Subtract the smaller from the larger (63 − 36 = 27). Now do this for two more pairs of digits and record the results in a table. What do you notice about all your answers?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All results are multiples of 9. For digit difference 1 the result is 9; for difference 2 it is 18; for difference 3 it is 27; and so on — the result equals 9 times the digit difference.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the reversed number from the original for several digit pairs and observe that every result is a multiple of 9, with the multiple equal to the digit difference.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student the completed first row of the table and ask them only to fill rows for two more examples; stretch: ask them to predict the result for a digit pair with difference 8 without computing, and check it.

exercise.description: Digit-swap subtraction puzzle: observe differences in each step; try other digit pairs; identify digits giving 1-digit number in first step; extend Mira's table for differences 2,3,5,7; find relationship between digit difference and number difference.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Find all the whole-number multiples of 1,000 that lie strictly between 44,500 and 51,500. List them in increasing order.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify that multiples of 1,000 have the form ___,000; list those between 44,500 and 51,500 by stepping in thousands.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student first to write every multiple of 1,000 from 40,000 to 55,000 and then circle those inside the given range; stretch: ask how many multiples of 1,000 lie between any two consecutive multiples of 10,000.

exercise.description: Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Fill in the blank: 4,350 = 3 Thousands + ___ Hundreds + 5 Tens + 0 Ones. Explain how you found the number of hundreds.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 13 Hundreds. 3 Thousands = 3,000; 4,350 − 3,000 = 1,350; 1,350 ÷ 100 = 13 Hundreds remainder 50 (the 5 Tens + 0 Ones). So the blank is 13.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the thousands portion from the total, then divide the remainder by 100 to find the non-standard hundreds count.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a place-value chart and ask the student to first write 4,350 in standard form before regrouping; stretch: ask them to write a second non-standard decomposition of 4,350 using 2 Thousands instead of 3.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions: e.g. 68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones; 607 = 4 Hundreds + __ Ones; 5,621 = 4 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 2 Tens + __ Ones; and similar (b)–(g).

items.prompt: Horses are placed around a square stable so that each side shows exactly 4 horses. The king counts 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16. How many horses are actually in the stable?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 12. With 4 horses on each side, place 1 horse at each corner (shared by 2 sides) and 2 horses along each of the 4 sides: 4 corners + 4 × 2 side horses = 4 + 8 = 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that corner horses are counted for two sides; total = 4 corners + (4 − 2) × 4 side horses = 4 + 8 = 12.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 4 × 4 = 16 without realising corner horses are shared between two sides — the direct double-counting error.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted one horse per side (4 × 3 = 12... miscalculated as 8) or counted only the non-corner horses — a partial correction applied incorrectly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student subtracted only two corner horses from 16 instead of four, partially recognising the shared-corner issue.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a drawn square with dots at corners and along sides and ask them to circle which dots appear on two sides; stretch: ask them to find the number of horses if each side must show 6, and whether there is more than one valid arrangement.

exercise.description: Count horses in the given arrangement and find the caretaker's mistake; arrange 18 horses with 5 on each side; explore how many more can be stolen before the king notices.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly writes the number name for 47,306?

options.label: B
options.text: Forty-seven thousand three hundred and six

options.label: C
options.text: Four lakh seventy-three hundred and six

options.label: D
options.text: Four thousand seven hundred and thirty-six

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Forty-seven thousand three hundred and six.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the number column by column from the place-value chart: TTh=4, Th=7 gives forty-seven thousand; H=3, T=0, O=6 gives three hundred and six.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflated the lakh system or misread the TTh digit as a lakh value — a misapplication of a higher place than the chapter introduces.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student read only the last four digits and ignored the TTh digit entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student omitted the hundreds value (300), collapsing it into zero and reading only the tens and ones.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write 47,306 in a place-value chart and name each column separately before joining; stretch: ask them to write the number name for 70,030 and explain which place-value columns are zero.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks appropriately: given a number write its number name, or given a name write the number; use commas as required.

items.prompt: What is 6,482 rounded to the nearest hundred?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 6,500. The hundreds benchmarks are 6,400 and 6,500. The tens digit is 8, so 6,482 is closer to 6,500.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the two nearest hundreds benchmarks, check the tens digit, and choose the closer benchmark.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student rounded down regardless of the tens digit — applying a wrong 'always round down' rule.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student rounded to the nearest thousand instead of nearest hundred.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student rounded to the nearest ten rather than the nearest hundred.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to mark 6,482 on a number line between 6,400 and 6,500 and count jumps to each end; stretch: ask them to find a number that rounds to 6,500 to the nearest hundred and also to 7,000 to the nearest thousand.

exercise.description: Complete the rabbit fill-in (nearest hundred and nearest thousand of 2,346); fill in the table giving nearest tens, hundreds, and thousands for 3,176; 4,017; 5,789; 8,203.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Which shows 45,070 correctly written in expanded form?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — 40,000 + 5,000 + 70. The hundreds and ones are both zero and are omitted from the expanded form.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write each non-zero digit multiplied by its place value and join with addition; omit zero-value terms.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student wrote the correct values but included zero terms — the chapter's convention is to omit zero-value place terms from expanded form.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student combined the ten-thousands and thousands as 45,000 and then misread the hundreds and tens as 700 — a place-shift error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student placed the 5 in the hundreds column instead of the thousands column, misreading the place-value position.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to fill a place-value chart for 45,070 first and then write only the non-zero columns; stretch: ask them to write 45,070 in a non-standard form using 3 ten-thousands instead of 4.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Arrange these prices in ascending (increasing) order: ₹52,100; ₹49,875; ₹52,010; ₹39,999; ₹62,000.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — ₹39,999 < ₹49,875 < ₹52,010 < ₹52,100 < ₹62,000. The two 52,___  numbers are distinguished by their hundreds: 52,010 has 0 hundreds and 52,100 has 1 hundred.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare column by column from the ten-thousands digit; for equal ten-thousands and thousands, move to hundreds to distinguish 52,010 from 52,100.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student swapped the order of ₹52,010 and ₹52,100 — comparing by the last three digits as a block rather than column by column.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student placed ₹49,875 before ₹39,999, reversing their order — possibly comparing the leading digit 4 against 3 but in the wrong direction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly ordered four numbers but placed ₹62,000 between the two 52,___ numbers — ignoring the ten-thousands digit of 62,000.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write all five numbers in a place-value chart and circle the ten-thousands digit of each before ordering; stretch: ask them to insert one more number between ₹52,010 and ₹52,100 and explain why it belongs there.

items.prompt: A school has 540 students going on a trip. Each bus carries 45 students. How many buses are needed to take all the students?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total number of students by the capacity of one bus.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first work out how many students 5 buses carry, then extend the pattern; stretch: ask what the minimum number of buses is if 3 students are added to the group, and whether they need a full extra bus or can fit within the existing 12.

exercise.description: A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them using modes (a) Bicycle(2) through (h) Aeroplane(180)?

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Anita has ₹8,650. She wants to change all of it into ₹100 notes. How many ₹100 notes will she get?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 86 notes. ₹8,650 ÷ ₹100 = 86 (with ₹50 remaining, which cannot form a ₹100 note). So she gets 86 complete ₹100 notes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total amount by 100; the quotient gives the number of complete ₹100 notes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first work out how many ₹100 notes make ₹1,000, then count how many thousands are in ₹8,650; stretch: ask how many ₹100 notes and how many extra ₹50 notes together make exactly ₹8,650.

exercise.description: Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934 and ₹65,342; how many thousands in each (b)–(h).
